content: Antiretroviral medications such as rilpivirine (Edurant), nelfinavir (Viracept), or saquinavir (Invirase), which are used to treat HIV or AIDS, may interact with other drugs. St. John’s Wort and rifampin, a medication commonly used to treat tuberculosis, can also interact with certain medications. Some drugs may alter the blood levels of omeprazole, and omeprazole may similarly affect the levels of other medications. It is essential to inform your healthcare provider about all medications you are currently taking or have recently taken, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and other supplements. Omeprazole may influence the absorption of certain medications, so it is crucial to discuss this with your healthcare provider. If you or someone else accidentally takes too much omeprazole, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose of omeprazole, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. The most common side effects of omeprazole include headache, stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, gas, and, in children aged 1 to 16 years, infections in the nose or throat and fever. If any of these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your healthcare provider if you suspect you are experiencing a side effect. You can also report side effects to the FDA at 800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 866-234-2345. Serious side effects of omeprazole, though less common, include kidney problems such as acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, which can occur at any time during treatment. If you notice a decrease in urine output or blood in your urine, contact your doctor immediately. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) can also occur. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever. Severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) or Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) may occur, which can be life-threatening. If you develop a rash, stop taking omeprazole and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Seek emergency help if you experience symptoms such as painful red or purple skin that peels, flat red rashes or blisters, or red, watery eyes. Omeprazole can also cause a severe allergic reaction known as DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), which may affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms include skin rash, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the legs or feet, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Stop using the medication and seek immediate medical attention if you experience these symptoms. In rare cases, omeprazole may cause or worsen lupus, an autoimmune disorder. Notify your provider if you develop new or worsening joint pain or a rash on your arms or cheeks. Long-term use of omeprazole (three years or more) may lead to vitamin B-12 deficiency, which can cause symptoms such as a sore tongue, weakness, or tingling in the hands or feet. Omeprazole may also cause low magnesium levels (hypomagnesemia), which can result in seizures, heart rhythm problems, dizziness, or muscle spasms. Bone loss and fractures are potential risks, particularly in older adults or those taking high doses or using the medication long-term. Omeprazole should not be used by individuals allergic to its ingredients, including other proton pump inhibitors. Before starting omeprazole, inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and OTC medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are using. Omeprazole may interact with medications such as clopidogrel (Plavix), cilostazol (Pletal), citalopram, methotrexate, digoxin (Lanoxin), warfarin, certain antiretroviral drugs, St. John’s Wort, and rifampin. Always discuss potential interactions with your healthcare provider. Do not take omeprazole unless prescribed by a healthcare provider. Take it as directed and do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition. Keep it out of reach of children. Do not chew, cut, or crush omeprazole capsules. If you have difficulty swallowing, you may open the capsule and sprinkle its contents on one tablespoon of applesauce, swallowing it immediately without mixing it with other foods. Omeprazole is not intended for immediate relief of heartburn and may take 1 to 4 days to take full effect. Before using omeprazole, inform your healthcare provider about any health conditions, including low blood potassium (hypokalemia), low magnesium (hypomagnesemia), low calcium (hypocalcemia), or liver problems. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss this with your provider, as omeprazole may pass into breast milk and its effects on pregnancy are not fully known.
